---
title: "Limitations"
description: "When each OPDI item is missing or can be wrong, what not to conclude from it, and where it is reliable."
---

OPDI is built from the position reports that the receivers of the OpenSky
Network pick up. Most of its limits come from that: where no receiver hears
an aircraft, nothing can be computed. This page lists the limits of every
published item. How each item is computed is on [Algorithms](algorithms/index.qmd);
how often it exists and how close it is to the records, overall and per
airport, is on [Accuracy and availability](accuracy/index.qmd).

**Found is not the same as correct.** An event that exists can still be
wrong, and an event that is missing says nothing about what the aircraft did.

## Summary

| Item | Main limits | Where it is reliable |
|---|---|---|
| [Tracks](#lim-tracks) (`flight_id`) | A track can hold several flights or part of one; placeholder addresses merge aircraft. | Airliners with continuous reception and a call sign per flight. |
| [Airports](#lim-airports) (`adep`, `ades`) | Small airfields and heliports never named; arrivals lost far out get no destination. | Medium and large airports, and rows whose source is `runway_event`. |
| [Aircraft details](#lim-aircraft) | Database of October 2024; type missing for about one flight in six. | Airliners registered before late 2024. |
| [First and last seen](#lim-first-last-seen) (`first_seen`, `last_seen`) | Describe reception, not the flight. | Everywhere, as reception times. |
| [Milestone columns](#lim-flight-list-milestones) | As available as their events; one take-off and one landing per row. | Where the events themselves are reliable. |
| [Take-off and landing](#lim-take-off-landing) (`ATOT`, `ALDT`) | Need reception near the runway; runway-window times (`legacy`) are less precise. | Airports with reception down to the runway; times with `info.method` = `acdm`. |
| [Other runway events](#lim-runway) (`line-up`, `take-off-roll`, `xing-runway-threshold`, `runway-vacated`, `go-around`, `runway-crossing-entry`, `runway-crossing-vacated`) | Need reports on the runway; placed at the first or last report when reception starts or ends there. | Airports with ground reception on the runways. |
| [Block times](#lim-block-times) (`AOBT`, `AIBT`) | Need reception at the stand; off-block late when first received moving. | Airports with dense ground reception and named stands in OpenStreetMap. |
| [Airport surface](#lim-surface) (`entry-{element}`, `exit-{element}`) | Need ground reception and a mapped layout; vehicles carry transponders. | Large airports with good ground reception and a detailed map. |
| [Vertical profile](#lim-vertical) (`top-of-climb`, `top-of-descent`, `level-start`, `level-end`, `level-off-climb-start`, `level-off-climb-end`, `level-off-descent-start`, `level-off-descent-end`, `xing-fl{level}`) | Not validated; slow aircraft and tracks cut by reception give odd profiles. | Jet airliners with a cruise, tracks with `info.observed` true. |
| [Distance circles](#lim-rings) (`xing-{radius}nm`) | Only around the row's two airports; position steps near spoofing. | The 40 and 100 NM circles at airports with good reception around them. |
| [FIR crossings](#lim-fir) (`xing-fir`) | One AIRAC cycle for every day. | Lateral crossings in airspace with continuous reception. |
| [Holding](#lim-holding) (`holding-start`, `holding-end`) | Circling for other reasons meets the definition. | Holds with `info.context` = `arrival`. |
| [Point merge](#lim-point-merge) (`pms-leg-entry`, `pms-leg-exit`, `pms-merge-point`) | Only the airports in the reference table. | Airports in the table with good reception on the arcs. |
| [Measurements](#lim-measurements) (`distance_flown_nm`, `time_passed_s`) | Count from the start of the track, not of the flight. | Differences between two events of one flight. |

## General limits {#general-limits}

- **Reception.** OpenSky receivers are on the ground and hear aircraft in
  line of sight. Over oceans, deserts and remote areas there are few of them,
  and near the ground an aircraft is heard only close to a receiver. So events
  in cruise are found almost everywhere, events on the runway at fewer
  airports, and events at the stand at fewer still. Missing events on the
  ground mostly mean missing reception, not that nothing happened. The
  airports where ground events are nearly absent are listed under
  [Off-block and in-block times](#ground-events-nearly-absent).
- **Tracks that hold several flights.** When an aircraft lands and departs
  again under the same call sign while receivers hear it all the time on the
  ground, the two flights stay one track. The flight-list row names the
  track's first and last airports; the distance-circle crossings, block times
  and stands at the middle stop are not on the row (the runway events there
  are still published as events). A track keeps one top of climb and one top
  of descent, and one take-off time and one landing time per airport.
- **Placeholder addresses.** Some transponders send addresses such as
  `000000`, `000001` or `ffffff`. Several aircraft can then be merged into one
  track; such tracks are not flagged.
- **Airport records to the whole minute.** Most airport operator records give
  times to the minute, so a difference of less than about half a minute
  between OPDI and a record cannot be judged.
- **Position spoofing and jumps.** Near areas where satellite navigation is
  disturbed (GPS spoofing), positions can jump or step by 5 to 20 NM and stay.
  Jumps that imply more than 1,000 kt are left out of the crossings and the
  distance flown; a spoofed position that does not jump (a frozen position)
  still misleads the detectors.
- **Vehicles.** Airport vehicles and some towed aircraft carry transponders.
  Tracks that never leave the ground are marked `info.ground_only` on their
  surface events and get no block times, but they remain in the flight list.
- **Airports without a mapped layout.** Surface events, block times and
  stands need the airport's taxiways, aprons and stands in OpenStreetMap. An
  airport that is not mapped, or a stand drawn without a name, gives no event
  or no stand name.
- **Small airfields and heliports** are not candidate airports, so their
  flights have no departure or destination airport and no runway events.
- **Reference data only in Europe.** The records OPDI is compared with
  (airport operator records and Network Manager flight records) cover the
  European area. Outside it, only how often an item is found can be measured,
  not whether it is right.
- **FIR boundaries.** The FIR crossings use the airspace of AIRAC cycle 524
  (28 November to 26 December 2024) for every day.
- **Aircraft database.** Registrations, types and operators come from the
  OpenSky aircraft database of October 2024.
- **Plausibility checks** remove only events the track clearly contradicts; a
  wrong but plausible event stays.

## Tracks and flight identity {#lim-tracks}

### When it is missing

A flight that no receiver heard has no track. A flight heard only in pieces
far apart can be split into several tracks: a silence of more than
30 minutes is kept inside one track only when both sides look like the same
flight en route.

### When it can be wrong

A track can hold two flights (a turnaround under one call sign with continuous
ground reception, see [General limits](#general-limits)), or merge aircraft
that share a placeholder address. A call sign broadcast wrongly for a long
time can split a flight.

### What not to conclude from it

The number of tracks is not the number of flights: count with the
[movement columns](algorithms/movements.qmd). `flt_id` is the call sign
broadcast most often, which may differ from the filed flight plan.

## Departure and destination airports {#lim-airports}

### When it is missing

`adep` is empty when the first report is more than 30 NM from any candidate
airport or more than 15,000 ft above it (a track first heard in cruise), and
when a track first heard in the air descends. `ades` is empty when the track
ends without descending near a candidate airport (reception lost in cruise
or far out). Small airfields and heliports are never named. Over the three
days measured, [24.2 %]{.measured} of the flights had no `adep` and
[35.7 %]{.measured} no `ades`. At a few busy European airports OPDI names the
airport as destination for only a small share of the recorded arrivals (see
[Accuracy: where no take-off or landing time exists](accuracy/europe.qmd#no-times)).

### When it can be wrong

At airports close together the nearest airport can be the wrong one, though
the direction of flight decides between airports less than 2 NM apart. A
track holding two flights names its first and last airports only.

### What not to conclude from it

An empty airport is not an overflight in every case: it can be a flight to a
small airfield, or one whose end was not received. `adep_source` and
`ades_source` say how sure the answer is: `runway_event` is the most reliable.

## Aircraft details {#lim-aircraft}

### When it is missing

When the address is not in the OpenSky aircraft database of October 2024:
aircraft registered later, military aircraft and many light aircraft. Over
the three days measured, [17.2 %]{.measured} of the flights the Network
Manager records had no type in OPDI.

### When it can be wrong

When an address moved to another aircraft after October 2024, or the
database entry is wrong.

### What not to conclude from it

`icao_operator` is the registered operator of the aircraft, not necessarily
the airline that flew the flight (wet leases, code shares).

## First seen and last seen {#lim-first-last-seen}

### When it is missing

Never: every track has both. A track without any measured position takes
them from its measured altitude or speed. They are identical in the flight
list and in the events.

### When it can be wrong

They are exact as reception times. A track that holds several flights has
one pair.

### What not to conclude from it

They are not the off-block or in-block times, nor the take-off or landing:
they are when the receivers first and last heard the aircraft.

## Milestone columns and movements {#lim-flight-list-milestones}

### When it is missing

A column is empty when its event was not found (see the event's section
below). `aobt`, `aibt` and the stand columns are often empty because they need
reception at the stand.

### When it can be wrong

As wrong as the event behind it. On a track holding several flights, the
events at the middle stop are not on the row. On a row with no departure
(or destination) airport, `aobt` and `stnd_dep` (or `aibt` and `stnd_arr`)
can still come from a block time read at a named stand; there is then no
airport to check them against.

### What not to conclude from it

The movement columns (`superseded_*`, `movement_*`) have not been checked
against official counts; two real short flights of one aircraft within
3 hours at one airport can be counted as one.

## Take-off and landing times {#lim-take-off-landing}

### When it is missing

When the aircraft was not received near the runway: the runway-pass method
needs reports on the runway or less than 1 NM short of it, the runway-window
method reports within 5 NM and 1,500 ft of the airport. Airports far from any
receiver have few times. In particular:

- a landing whose reception ends in the flare, before any report on the
  runway, can get no landing time;
- a take-off first received more than 1,500 ft above the track's ground
  altitude at the airport gets no take-off time;
- at some busy European airports OPDI has no take-off or landing time at all
  on the three days measured; they are listed on
  [Accuracy: where no take-off or landing time exists](accuracy/europe.qmd#no-times).
  The cause has not been established.

### When it can be wrong

- Runway-window times (`info.method` = `legacy`) are the first or last report
  of the climb or descent, so they are less precise. Over the three days
  measured, [94.3 %]{.measured} of the runway-pass take-off times and
  [91.5 %]{.measured} of the runway-window ones were within 60 s of the
  airport records; for landings, [97.1 %]{.measured} and [87.9 %]{.measured}.
  Where reception starts at lift-off or ends over the threshold, the time
  comes from a report up to 1,500 ft above the ground;
  `info.at_track_edge` marks the first or last report of the track.
- At a few airports the runway named, or the take-off time, mostly disagrees
  with the records; they are listed on
  [Accuracy: where an item is unreliable](accuracy/europe.qmd#unreliable).
- When the track has no ground report at the airport, the height is measured
  above the published elevation, which on a day of low or high pressure moves
  the 15 ft crossing (`info.height_reference` = `elevation`).

### What not to conclude from it

The two methods have different errors: separate them with `info.method` when
comparing airports. A track keeps one `ATOT` and one `ALDT` per airport: on
a track that holds several flights, a second take-off or landing at the same
airport is not published.

## Other runway events {#lim-runway}

### When it is missing

`line-up`, `take-off-roll` and `runway-vacated` need a report on the runway
itself; where reception starts at lift-off or ends over the threshold, they
are not published. `line-up` and `take-off-roll` are not given for a
touch-and-go or a low approach. `xing-runway-threshold` needs reports in the
last minute before the runway and at most 300 ft above the ground there.
Runway crossings need ground reception on the runway.

### When it can be wrong

When reception starts during the take-off roll or ends during the landing
roll, `line-up`, `take-off-roll` and `runway-vacated` mark the first or last
report received on the runway, which can be at high speed. A go-around
detector based on heights can count a training low approach, and misses
go-arounds started above 1,500 ft.

### What not to conclude from it

No reference gives line-up, take-off roll, runway vacated, go-around or
runway crossing times; these events are not validated, only compared with the
recorded take-off or landing.

## Off-block and in-block times {#lim-block-times}

### When it is missing

Often: they need reception at the stand and on the taxiway, and a stand
passage in the track. An arrival with no position or speed after the landing
roll gets no in-block time. Over the three days measured,
[35.0 %]{.measured} of the recorded off-blocks had an `AOBT` and
[33.4 %]{.measured} of the recorded in-blocks an `AIBT`.

::: {#ground-events-nearly-absent}
At these airports of the 100 busiest in Europe, fewer than 2 % of OPDI's
departures have an off-block time and fewer than 2 % of its arrivals an
in-block time: block times, stands and the airport surface events are
nearly absent there. Take-off and landing times can still exist.

{{< include accuracy/_generated/europe_ground.md >}}
:::

### When it can be wrong

- When the transponder is switched on during the push-back, or the aircraft
  is first received already moving, the off-block time is the first movement
  received, which is late. A push slower than 2 kt, or a stand with few
  reports with a position, also gives a late off-block time.
- Off-block times are often late: over the three days measured, the median
  difference from the airport records is [99 s]{.measured}, and over the
  differences of up to 300 s OPDI is on average [78.6 s]{.measured} later
  than the record. In-block times are closer: a median difference of
  [34 s]{.measured}, and on average [18.5 s]{.measured} earlier than the
  record over the differences of up to 300 s.
- A stand drawn in OpenStreetMap without a name gives no stand name. Where a
  stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, the block times read the inner
  one.

### What not to conclude from it

A missing block time does not mean the aircraft did not park. Taxi times from
`AOBT` are more often too short than too long, because a late `AOBT` is the
common error.

## Airport surface events {#lim-surface}

### When it is missing

At airports without ground reception or without a mapped layout in
OpenStreetMap. An area mapped without a name gives no `info.osm_ref`.

### When it can be wrong

- Vehicles carry transponders: tracks that never leave the ground with no
  aircraft type, or a vehicle type, are marked `info.ground_only`.
- An entry at the first report of a track or an exit at its last is when
  reception started or stopped (`info.at_track_start`, `info.at_track_end`),
  not a movement.
- Where a stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, both passages are
  published; the larger carries `info.encloses_stand`.

### What not to conclude from it

A `deicing_pad` event means the pad area was passed, not that the aircraft
was de-iced. `entry-threshold` and `exit-threshold` are aircraft on the ground
near the threshold markings (lining up), not the landing crossing of the
threshold, which is `xing-runway-threshold`.

## Vertical profile {#lim-vertical}

### When it is missing

Level-offs need both tops. Tops need altitudes in the air; a flight-level
crossing needs reports with altitude either side of the level within
30 minutes. A flight that levels off at a crossed level itself has no
crossing of it. No level segment is published on reports flagged on the
ground, or less than 200 ft above an airport within 10 NM of it.

### When it can be wrong

- A flight without a cruise (short, training) gets its highest report as
  tops; a track holding several flights gets one pair. A top at the edge of
  reception has `info.observed` = false.
- The cruise of light aircraft splits into many level segments and
  level-offs, and the flight phases of slow aircraft are less reliable.
- A crossing between reports far apart in time is an estimate: see
  `info.bracket_s`.

### What not to conclude from it

None of these events is compared with a reference: no record gives tops,
level segments or level crossings.

## Distance circles {#lim-rings}

### When it is missing

When the flight has no departure or destination airport, or reception does
not cover the circle. On a track holding several flights the middle stop has
no circles.

### When it can be wrong

Near areas of GPS spoofing a position can step by 5 to 20 NM and stay. A
crossing across such a step is kept when it passes one circle only and is
marked `info.position_jump`; larger steps give no crossing. Circles are drawn
on every leg of a track that holds several flights.

### What not to conclude from it

Only the 40 and 100 NM circles are compared with airport records; the others
are not validated.

## FIR crossings {#lim-fir}

### When it is missing

Where no position is received (oceans), and for stays shorter than 60 s in a
region, which count as part of the region before.

### When it can be wrong

The boundaries are those of AIRAC cycle 524 for every day. A crossing placed
between two reports far apart in time (`info.bracket_s`) is an estimate.

### What not to conclude from it

A crossing with `info.vertical` = true is a climb or descent between a lower
and an upper region, not a lateral boundary crossing.

## Holding {#lim-holding}

### When it is missing

Holds below 2,500 ft above the airport, slower than 140 kt or shorter than
240 s are not found, nor holds cut by a reception gap.

### When it can be wrong

Aerial work, survey, firefighting and training flights that circle meet the
definition; they usually get `info.context` = `other`.

### What not to conclude from it

Not every hold is arrival delay: use `info.context` = `arrival` for delay
statistics.

## Point merge {#lim-point-merge}

### When it is missing

Only arrivals at the airports in the reference table are examined. A leg cut
by a reception gap, or shorter than 90 s, is missed.

### When it can be wrong

At airports with several systems close together, a leg can be given to the
wrong merge point; `pms-merge-point` is linked to the runway landed on only
where the system's name says which runway it serves.

### What not to conclude from it

`pms-merge-point` with `info.via_leg` false is an arrival that passed the merge
point without a leg being found, not necessarily one sent direct.

## Measurements {#lim-measurements}

### When it is missing

`distance_flown_nm` is empty before the first known position, and on tracks
without any position. `time_passed_s` is empty on an event earlier than
`first_seen`.

### When it can be wrong

Across a reception gap the distance adds the straight line, so it is a lower
bound. A position jump that implies more than 1,000 kt is not added.

### What not to conclude from it

Both count from the start of the track, not from the off-block or the
take-off: a track first received in the air starts later. Use differences
between two events of the same flight.
